Evolution timing can affect which techniques become available. A useful planning detail.
No need to rush a change when the team has a reason to wait.
I like hearing that waiting can be a real choice.
A little patience now can give a partner more to work with later.
A delayed transformation can still be progress. An excellent complication.
Something can keep learning without becoming something else yet.
Sequence matters! Learn the useful thing, then consider the next stage.
There are more ways to grow than changing shape.
Timing can be part of the plan. Faster is not automatically better.
I wonder which Pokemon taught that trainer to pay attention to the timing.

contexts.subject: The laboratory researcher describes daily study and rare Pokemon visitors.

CinnabarIsland_PokemonLab_Entrance_Text_.text: We study POKéMON extensively\nevery day.\pPeople often bring us rare POKéMON\nfor examination.$

replies.text: People bring rare Pokemon right to work? That would improve any Monday.
A steady stream of unusual specimens could make comparative research very productive.
Hope the visitors are handled carefully. Rare still means living.
It must be exciting to arrive without knowing what someone will bring that day.
That sounds like work that rewards patience as much as excitement.
Their ordinary working day includes somebody else's extraordinary discovery.
A room where strange arrivals are expected. Rather welcoming, in its own way.
New observations every day! I would need so many notebooks.
People carry their mysteries here and ask for names.
An interesting place to work, especially if the team shares what it learns.
I would love to hear which recent visitor surprised them most.

contexts.subject: A lab scientist describes three possible Eevee evolutions.

CinnabarIsland_PokemonLab_ResearchRoom_T.text: EEVEE can evolve into one of three\nkinds of POKéMON.$

replies.text: One small Pokemon, three very different futures. That is a busy decision.
Eevee is unusually responsive to different evolutionary conditions.
Worth thinking about the partner and the team before choosing a direction.
Three possibilities can be exciting and a little daunting.
There is time to get to know Eevee before making a big decision.
A single beginning offers a remarkably generous selection of next chapters.
A creature with several possible silhouettes. I understand the fascination.
One starting point, multiple outcomes. No wonder researchers find Eevee interesting.
Several futures curled inside the same small body.
It is easy to imagine each version. Harder to choose just one.
I wonder which possibility the researcher finds most interesting.

contexts.subject: A visitor believes a Mt. Moon fossil belonged to a rare prehistoric Pokemon.

CinnabarIsland_PokemonLab_Lounge_Text_Fo.text: I found this most remarkable fossil\ninside MT. MOON.\pI think it's of a rare, prehistoric\nPOKéMON.$

replies.text: A piece of mountain that used to be somebody. That is quite a find.
The identification is tentative, but a well-preserved fossil could offer valuable evidence.
Handle it carefully. One careless bump could ruin a remarkable find.
Their excitement is quiet, but you can hear how much the discovery matters.
Good that they brought it somewhere people can examine it properly.
Mt. Moon has surrendered a very old character from a very incomplete story.
Something ancient survived long enough for someone to be delighted by it.
A natural record preserved inside the rock! I would be staring too.
The mountain kept a shape the living world forgot.
Calling it remarkable before being certain what it is feels rather honest.
I wonder what first caught their eye among all the ordinary stone.

contexts.subject: The fossil scientist asks us to wait while resurrection is in progress.

CinnabarIsland_PokemonLab_ExperimentRoom.text: I take a little time!\nYou go for walk a little while!$

replies.text: Bringing back ancient life takes a little while. Apparently we should stretch our legs.
An extraordinary process still needs time. We should let the researcher work.
No point hovering. We can come back when the work is ready.
Waiting feels strange when the thing you are waiting for is so enormous.
A short walk is better than crowding somebody doing delicate work.
The ancient world is being restored; meanwhile, we have been assigned a stroll.
Something absent for so long can keep us waiting a little longer.
Important work in progress. Resist the urge to ask every ten seconds.
A very old silence is taking its time becoming a heartbeat.
The doctor is brisk, but at least the instruction is clear.
I wonder how the lab sounds when the machine begins its work.

contexts.subject: The fossil scientist invites another visit after a refusal or completed fossil work.

replies.text: The invitation survived the very abrupt delivery. We can come back.
That leaves the conversation open without requiring another decision now.
We are done here for now. He knows where to find us: eventually, back here.
A short goodbye. I think he means it kindly.
We can leave him to his research and return when we have a reason.
A farewell stripped to its essential instruction: make another entrance someday.
A door left open in very few words.
Brief, reusable, difficult to misinterpret. Efficient farewell.
He sends us away without quite closing the door.
He does not waste syllables on goodbyes, does he?
He seems more comfortable with another visit than a long conversation.

contexts.subject: A local describes the active Safari Warden and mentions his false teeth.

FuchsiaCity_House1_Text_WardenIsOldHasFa.text: The SAFARI ZONE's WARDEN is old, \nbut he's still very much active.\pAll his teeth are false, though.$

replies.text: Apparently the Warden has more energy than his original teeth had staying power.
Dental replacements tell us little about someone's ability to manage a reserve.
He is still active. That is the part that matters for his work.
An oddly personal detail to offer a visitor.
Staying busy doing something you care about sounds good at any age.
A professional biography with a sudden detour into dentistry.
He has outlasted his teeth. There is a certain stubborn dignity in that.
Replacement parts, continued operation. Nothing wrong with that.
An old keeper, still making his rounds. Teeth are a separate matter.
She could have stopped at active. Town gossip rarely knows where to stop.
People here certainly know the Warden's everyday details.

contexts.subject: Bill's grandfather recalls that Bill collected things as a child.

FuchsiaCity_House1_Text_BillIsMyGrandson.text: Hmm?\nYou've met BILL?\pHe's my grandson!\pHe always liked collecting things,\neven as a child!$

replies.text: The impressive grown-up was once a kid bringing more things home. That tracks.
A childhood interest persisted and became much more organized over time.
Sounds like his family saw the beginnings long before anyone else did.
His grandfather sounds pleased that we know him.
I like hearing the small beginning behind somebody's big reputation.
A famous name briefly becomes somebody's grandson with an overfull collection.
It is nice when a person's old strangeness becomes something their family treasures.
Early collecting habits scaled up impressively. I sympathize with the storage problem.
A child kept things. Years later, people kept his name in mind.
There is pride in the way he says grandson. Very little disguise on it.
I wonder what Bill collected before Pokemon took over his attention.

contexts.subject: A child admires Bill recording his Pokemon data on his own PC.

FuchsiaCity_House1_Text_BillFilesHisOwnM.text: BILL files his own POKéMON data on\nhis PC.\pDid he show you?$

replies.text: Collecting the facts as well as the Pokemon. That is a second collection hiding inside the first.
Personal records can preserve observations that broad references overlook.
Keeping track makes it easier to care for what you have.
The boy sounds impressed by the care behind the collection.
A record is only useful if somebody takes the time to maintain it.
Bill seems unwilling to let an interesting detail escape without being filed.
An orderly place for all the little things someone else might forget.
A personal database! Now I want to know how he organizes the entries.
A machine full of carefully kept little traces of living things.
The child noticed the work, not just the impressive collection. Good eye.
I wonder whether Bill showed him how the system works.

contexts.subject: After giving the Good Rod, the fishing guru's brother explains its broader catches.

FuchsiaCity_House2_Text_GoodRodCanCatchB.text:
Fishing is a way of life!
It is like the finest poetry.\pA crummy OLD ROD could only catch
MAGIKARP, yes?\pBut with a GOOD ROD, you can
catch much better POKéMON.$

replies.text: A better rod and a speech about poetry. Fishing comes with a surprisingly full service.
Different equipment changes the range of Pokemon we might encounter.
Better tool, more options. Still need patience.
He shared something he loves instead of just telling us to try it.
That was generous. We can make good use of it without matching his enthusiasm immediately.
He has equipped a new disciple and delivered the opening verse.
He finds poetry in waiting beside water. I can respect that.
A practical upgrade, personally endorsed by somebody gloriously biased.
A line can reach a little farther into the unknown now.
He calls it a way of life and actually gives people a way to begin.
I wonder what catch made him love fishing this much.

contexts.subject: The fishing enthusiast is disappointed that we do not share his interest.

replies.text: We have gently punctured a very fish-shaped dream.
Shared enthusiasm would please him, but it cannot be assumed.
He asked. We answered. No need to pretend.
It is hard to disappoint someone who was so ready to be excited.
He will find another person eager to talk rods and water.
The proposed fishing fellowship has met a polite administrative obstacle.
Not every visitor is a future fishing companion. A small, survivable tragedy.
Enthusiasm is not universal. An unfortunate constraint on recruiting hobbyists.
The water can keep its invitation for another person.
He took that personally, but at least he accepted the answer.
I wonder how many conversations here begin and end with fishing.

contexts.subject: The fishing enthusiast greets us by name and asks about our catches.

FuchsiaCity_House2_Text_HowAreTheFishBit.text: Hello there, {PLAYER}!\pHow are the fish biting?$

replies.text: He remembers us! We have become part of the fishing report.
He is following up on an interest he helped us explore.
Nice that he remembers who he gave the rod to.
A familiar greeting makes coming back feel easier.
That sounds like a real invitation to stay and compare stories.
We return as acquaintances, expected to bring news from the water.
His world has room for one more person and their small fishing failures.
A follow-up question after handing over equipment. Good support!
The river has become a reason for him to remember our name.
He made the greeting personal. That is how a hobby becomes company.
I suspect he enjoys hearing about a catch almost as much as making one.

contexts.subject: A shopper wants Safari Zone pennants, lanterns, or calendars.

FuchsiaCity_Mart_Text_DontTheyHaveSafari.text: Don't they have any pennants\npromoting the SAFARI ZONE?\pHow about some paper lanterns?\nAren't there even any calendars?$

replies.text: They have assembled a complete souvenir wish list and found none of it.
There seems to be unmet demand for merchandise beyond practical trainer supplies.
A calendar seems harmless. Better than trying to take a whole fence sign home.
They want a little reminder of the place. I understand that.
A local keepsake would make a nice gift for somebody who could not come.
The reserve has inspired a merchandising vision this shop cannot fulfill.
They want to carry the memory home in paper rather than a ball.
Clear demand, three product ideas, zero stock. Someone is missing a market!
A paper lantern can hold a place in someone's memory surprisingly well.
They even offered alternatives. That is a committed souvenir shopper.
I wonder which scene they would want on the calendar.

contexts.subject: A shopper recommends X Speed for raising Speed in battle.

FuchsiaCity_Mart_Text_DidYouTryXSpeed.text: Did you try X SPEED?\nIt speeds up a POKéMON in battle.$

replies.text: A whole bottle of hurry. Useful, provided we know when to open it.
A temporary Speed increase can change which combatant acts first.
Useful if getting the first move changes the fight.
They sound pleased to have found something that worked for them.
Good to know what the bottle does before a hurried battle decision.
The shop offers haste in conveniently portable form.
Speed, briefly borrowed from a bottle. A peculiar little advantage.
Changing action order can change the whole plan. Small item, big timing effect.
A moment can matter more than a great deal of force.
A clear recommendation. Refreshing after the shelves of vague promises.
I wonder which battle made them start recommending it to strangers.

contexts.subject: A trainer warns against relying on one strong Pokemon while admitting balanced training is hard.

FuchsiaCity_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_CantBe.text: You can't become a good TRAINER\nwith just one strong POKéMON.\pBut raising many POKéMON evenly\nis no easy task, either.$

replies.text: One hero cannot carry the whole picnic forever. Especially if the picnic fights back.
Distributing training reduces dependence on a single partner, though it takes more time.
One exhausted partner is a weak backup plan. Share the work.
I appreciate that they admitted the difficult part instead of making it sound easy.
Everybody needs a turn and a rest. Keeping that balance takes attention.
An ensemble demands more rehearsal than a solo act, and survives more surprises.
Depending on one strong partner puts a quiet weight on that partner.
A system with one point of failure needs better backup. Training is the costly part.
Let more than one set of shoulders learn the weight.
Sound advice, made better by admitting the effort it asks for.
I wonder whether they learned this after their strongest partner had a bad day.

contexts.subject: A visitor describes the League headquarters reached west of Viridian.

FuchsiaCity_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_Pokemo.text: There's a narrow trail west of\nVIRIDIAN CITY.\pIt goes to the POKéMON LEAGUE HQ.\nThe HQ governs all TRAINERS.$

replies.text: A narrow trail to the people overseeing all those trainers. Busy little path.
Useful geographic information. The League's headquarters lie west of Viridian.
Worth knowing where it is before we need to make the trip.
A place that important begins with an ordinary trail. That feels strange.
That sounds like a journey to plan carefully, with supplies and time.
A modest turning in Viridian leads toward an institution with a very large reach.
A narrow path can carry a remarkable amount of ambition.
Regional headquarters at the end of a trail. Memorable navigation advice.
A small way west, then a great many expectations.
A useful direction from someone who assumes visitors may be aiming high.
I wonder how many travelers pass Viridian without noticing that trail.

contexts.subject: A visitor recommends the Safari Zone to Pokedex collectors for rare Pokemon.

FuchsiaCity_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_VisitS.text: If you're working on a POKéDEX,\nvisit the SAFARI ZONE.\pAll sorts of rare POKéMON breed\nthere.$

replies.text: A place full of new faces. Some may be better at leaving than introducing themselves.
A reserve with varied species could fill important gaps in a field record.
Prepare before going in. Rare sightings do not guarantee easy catches.
Even seeing something unfamiliar would make the trip interesting.
A good lead for the Pokedex. Bring patience along with the fee.
The local reserve offers an unusually lively appendix to our travels.
A place to meet creatures the roads have not introduced us to yet.
A concentrated observation opportunity! Worth keeping careful notes.
Some names wait behind the reserve's gates rather than along the road.
A recommendation tailored to what we might be trying to do. Helpful.
I wonder which zone gives visitors their most surprising first encounter.

contexts.subject: An employee says staff call the Warden Slowpoke because of his vacant expression.

FuchsiaCity_SafariZone_Office_Text_Nickn.text: We nicknamed the WARDEN\n“SLOWPOKE.”\pYou know, he has that vacant look\nlike a SLOWPOKE.$

replies.text: I wonder whether the Warden approved this very detailed performance review.
An expression is a poor measure of what someone is thinking.
A blank look does not mean an empty head.
I hope he finds the nickname as funny as they do.
Being familiar with somebody is not always the same as being kind to them.
The office has established a nickname on the strength of one facial expression.
Some of us look vacant while doing perfectly adequate worrying.
External display does not always show internal activity. Machines taught me that.
Quiet faces can conceal very busy weather.
A nickname works better when the person wearing it gets a say.
I wonder what the Warden calls the people in this office.

contexts.subject: An employee praises the Warden's Pokemon knowledge and fossil collection.

FuchsiaCity_SafariZone_Office_Text_Warde.text: WARDEN SLOWPOKE is very\nknowledgeable about POKéMON.\pHe even has some fossils of rare,\nextinct POKéMON.$

replies.text: A head full of Pokemon facts and a shelf full of ancient ones. Good combination.
His collection may reflect decades of sustained interest and careful study.
Experience and actual knowledge. Good qualities for the person running the place.
It is nice to hear someone recognize what he knows.
He must have plenty of stories behind those fossils.
The office nickname conceals a rather distinguished natural historian.
He keeps company with living creatures and traces of the vanished ones.
Fossils and field experience! I would have several questions ready.
Someone tending the living has kept room for the long absent.
That tells us much more about him than his expression does.
I wonder whether his rare fossils came from his own journeys.

contexts.subject: An employee could not understand the Warden when he visited the office.

FuchsiaCity_SafariZone_Office_Text_Could.text: WARDEN SLOWPOKE came in, but\nI couldn't understand him.\pI think he's got a speech problem!$

replies.text: That sounds frustrating for him too. Words get heavy when they will not come out right.
Difficulty producing clear speech does not imply difficulty understanding the situation.
Give him time. He is still trying to tell them something.
It is awful when people stop listening because the words are difficult.
They could try writing things down together instead of guessing at him.
A failed conversation has become gossip. I would rather hear whether anyone helped.
Being misunderstood in your own workplace sounds quietly miserable.
If one way of communicating fails, try another. Paper is not complicated equipment.
A message can be trapped at the very edge of being heard.
I hope they offered patience before giving the problem a name.
I wonder what he was trying so hard to tell them.

contexts.subject: An employee describes a prize for reaching the Safari Zone's farthest corner.

FuchsiaCity_SafariZone_Office_Text_Prize.text:
WARDEN SLOWPOKE is running a
promotion campaign right now.\pTry to get to the farthest corner
of the SAFARI ZONE.\pIf you can make it, you'll win a
very convenient prize.$

replies.text: A prize for getting thoroughly lost in the correct direction. Tempting.
We should study the layout before committing limited time to the farthest section.
Plan the route. Getting there means little if we waste the whole visit wandering.
A little goal might make exploring feel less aimless.
We can explore at a steady pace and see how far we get.
The Warden has placed convenience at a deliberately inconvenient distance.
A useful prize waiting in the farthest quiet corner. A good lure.
A navigation challenge with a practical reward! I am listening.
The far corner has a reason for us to find it.
They have made the promotion sound mysterious enough to work.
I wonder how many visitors find the prize by accident.

contexts.subject: Copycat imitates our side of the conversation and calls mimicry her favorite hobby.

SaffronCity_CopycatsHouse_2F_Text_Mimick.text:
{PLAYER}: Hi!
Do you like POKéMON?\p{PLAYER}: Uh, no, I just asked you.\p{PLAYER}: Huh?
You're strange!\pCOPYCAT: Hmm? Quit mimicking?
But, that's my favorite hobby!$

{PLAYER}: Hi.
You must like POKéMON.\p{PLAYER}: No, not me.
I asked you.\p{PLAYER}: Pardon?
You're weird!\l \lCOPYCAT: Hmm? Quit mimicking?\lBut that's my favorite hobby!$

replies.text: For a moment, there were twice as many of us and neither knew what to say.
Accurate imitation requires careful observation. The conversational confusion is substantial.
Clever trick. Still unsettling when somebody borrows your voice without warning.
Hearing your own hesitation from someone else is rather embarrassing.
She managed both sides of that exchange without needing much help.
An ambitious performance in which our role was taken from us mid-sentence.
I am relieved she has not discovered how little I say. Easy material to steal.
Fast turnaround on voice replication! Social consequences still under development.
An echo that lives in a house and enjoys itself.
She notices people closely. A little warning would improve the presentation.
I wonder how many tiny habits she picked up before we even spoke.

contexts.subject: Sebastian notices his birds are happy despite losing.

Route13_Text_SebastianPostBattle.text: My POKéMON look happy even though\nthey lost.$

replies.text: The birds enjoyed themselves. Their scoreboard may be entirely different from ours.
Their behavior matters more than assuming defeat made them unhappy.
Good. They worked hard and still had a decent time.
He noticed how they felt before worrying about the result.
A happy team after a loss is a good thing to bring home.
The trainer lost the match; the birds appear to have enjoyed the outing.
They have refused to make a tragedy of the afternoon. Sensible birds.
Actual feedback from the team beats guessing from a win-loss record.
Feathers do not have to droop just because the battle ended badly.
He is reading his Pokemon instead of just the result. Good instinct.
I like that he stopped to look at them and noticed their mood.

contexts.subject: Susie promises to train hard and become a good trainer.

Route13_Text_SusiePostBattle.text: I want to become a good TRAINER.\nI'll train hard, just watch.$

replies.text: She has already turned the loss into tomorrow's plan. Quick work.
Deliberate practice will help more than effort without direction.
Good resolve. Rest the team before putting it to work again.
She sounds determined without trying to pretend the loss did not happen.
A good trainer keeps learning and looks after the partners doing the work.
A declaration delivered to the nearest available witness. I believe her.
A little stubbornness can keep a bad afternoon from becoming an ending.
That is energy she can use. A clear training goal would give it direction.
She has planted the next attempt right inside this defeat.
She wants us to remember this. There is some real fire behind it.
I would be curious to see what changes when she tries again.

contexts.subject: Valerie recognizes that our badges came from Gym Leaders.

Route13_Text_ValeriePostBattle.text: You got those BADGES from GYM\nLEADERS. I know!$

replies.text: The badges have been successfully identified as badges. Investigation complete.
She recognizes what the badges represent, even if the explanation is familiar.
We earned them with the team. They are more than something shiny to wear.
She sounds delighted to have worked it out herself.
They carry a lot of effort for such small things.
Our credentials have passed a very enthusiastic visual inspection.
A tiny metal object can make a long struggle look deceptively neat.
Correct origin identified. I award her an imaginary badge for badge analysis.
Little marks of places where we stayed and tried.
Her excitement is sweet. A badge does make a good conversation starter.
I wonder which Gym Leader she would most like to challenge.

contexts.subject: Gwen says Pokemon need battle experience to become tougher.

Route13_Text_GwenPostBattle.text: You have to make POKéMON battle\nto toughen them up.$

replies.text: Practice helps. So does knowing when everybody has had enough practice.
Experience can improve performance when the challenge is appropriate and recovery is adequate.
Train them. Do not grind them down. There is a difference.
Learning through battles makes sense when the partners are ready for them.
Hard work needs proper rest on either side of it.
A reasonable principle, provided toughness is not measured by how much hurt one ignores.
Growing stronger should leave a creature with more than just new bruises.
Repeated testing helps if you learn from the results and allow repairs.
A living thing can harden without being treated like stone.
Good training takes judgment, not just more battles on the schedule.
I wonder how she decides her Pokemon have had a good day's practice.

contexts.subject: Alma says the Carbos she found increased her Pokemon's Speed.

Route13_Text_AlmaPostBattle.text: CARBOS boosted the SPEED of my\nPOKéMON.$

replies.text: A cave trip made her Pokemon quicker. My cave trips mostly make my socks wetter.
She put the find to use and observed a change in Speed.
Useful find. Good that it suited something her team needed.
She sounds pleased that exploring helped her partner.
Always satisfying when a lucky discovery becomes something practical.
The expedition yielded a measurable improvement rather than merely an impressive story.
A small bottle from a dark place changed the pace of her journey.
Exploration, useful material, observable result. Excellent little chain of events.
The cave held a little hurry in reserve.
She knows where it came from and what it did. A well-remembered find.
I wonder whether finding it made her more eager to explore other caves.

contexts.subject: Perry is tired after losing and decides to fly home.

Route13_Text_PerryPostBattle.text: I'm beat.\nI guess I'll FLY home.$

replies.text: He has chosen the skyward route to a quiet evening. Good exit.
Ending the outing while tired is a reasonable decision.
Heading home beats pushing an exhausted team another mile.
It sounds like he knows when to call it a day.
Home and a proper rest seem like a good next plan.
A defeat followed by a practical and admirably swift departure.
Some afternoons are best folded away before they get any longer.
Return route selected. Now make sure the bird is rested enough for the trip.
There is a particular comfort in seeing home from above.
A graceful exit does not have to pretend the day went well.
I wonder whether flying home is his favorite part of an outing.

contexts.subject: Lola wonders whether male or female Pokemon are stronger.

Route13_Text_LolaPostBattle.text: I wonder which is stronger, male or\nfemale POKéMON?$

replies.text: I would start by asking the actual Pokemon, rather than appointing a winning half.
A broad comparison conceals species, training, individual traits, and match conditions.
Judge the partner in front of you. That question is too broad.
It seems unfair to decide what someone can do before meeting them.
Training and care tell us much more about this team than that guess does.
A sweeping debate has arrived to distract us from one quite specific loss.
An entire category of Pokemon need not answer for this afternoon.
Too many uncontrolled variables. Also, several potential bites.
Living things rarely fit neatly into the boxes we make for them.
That is a very large conclusion to try to draw from one battle.
I would rather hear what surprised her about the particular opponents she faced.

contexts.subject: Sheila admits choosing her team for looks and knowing little about Pokemon.

Route13_Text_SheilaPostBattle.text: I don't know anything about\nPOKéMON actually.\pThe ones I use… I picked them\nfor their looks!$

replies.text: Looks got her interested. Now she has a whole team of reasons to learn more.
Visual preference can begin an interest; understanding their needs should follow.
Fine place to start. Learn what those partners can actually do.
Admitting what she does not know takes a little courage.
Liking them is a beginning. Caring well for them is the next part.
The cast was chosen for appearance. Now comes the rewarding work of knowing them.
Beauty opened the door. I hope curiosity gets a room too.
She has identified the knowledge gap. That is a workable starting point.
A pretty surface can invite you toward a much stranger interior.
Style caught her eye. Personality might be what makes her stay.
I wonder which one first made her stop and look.

contexts.subject: Jared angrily tells us to leave after losing.

replies.text: That sounds like our invitation to be somewhere else.
He has made his preference for ending the conversation sufficiently clear.
We are leaving. No need to give him another excuse.
I would rather let the conversation stop there.
A little distance seems good for everybody now.
A brief review of our presence, with no invitation for revisions.
An economical farewell. Rather lacking in charm.
Signal received, aggressively. Exit seems straightforward.
Some doors close themselves quite loudly.
He could have managed that with fewer sharp edges. We can go.
That is not a conversation likely to improve by staying.

contexts.subject: Robert wishes he could fly like Pidgey and Pidgeotto.

Route13_Text_RobertPostBattle.text: I wish I could fly like PIDGEY and\nPIDGEOTTO…$

replies.text: The birds make it look unfairly easy. My arms have received the complaint.
Watching flight can make its mechanical difficulty feel almost insulting.
A fair wish on a road this long.
I understand wanting that feeling, even for a little while.
A cool breeze and no tired feet. There is plenty to like in that idea.
An old human ambition, renewed by two birds doing it without ceremony.
To leave the ground without asking anything to carry you. Yes, I understand.
Wings solve a very tempting transport problem. Shame about the weight requirements.
The sky looks nearer when something small can reach it.
He admires them for something beyond winning battles. I like that.
I wonder whether he watches them fly even when they are just playing.

contexts.subject: Carter warns that HM moves cannot be forgotten easily.

Route14_Text_CarterPostBattle.text: You have some HMs, right? POKéMON\ncan't forget those moves easily.$

replies.text: A useful move can be a stubborn houseguest. Good to know before inviting it in.
The difficulty of removing an HM move makes the initial choice consequential.
Think before teaching it. Useful does not mean easy to replace.
That is the sort of detail I would rather hear before choosing.
A long-term choice deserves a little time, even when the move helps immediately.
A lesson with unusually persistent attendance. Read the commitment before enrolling.
Some knowledge lingers past the moment we wanted it. This kind quite literally.
A hard-to-reverse configuration change. Plan the slot first.
A useful thing can still take root where you did not mean it to stay.
Important advice, though he could have led with it before the battle.
I wonder how many trainers learn that rule only after trying to change a move.

contexts.subject: Mitch thinks his birds need a better selection of moves.

Route14_Text_MitchPostBattle.text: My bird POKéMON need to learn\nbetter moves.$

replies.text: He has found something to work on besides being cross with the birds. Good.
Reviewing move selection is a more specific response than simply demanding more strength.
Give them better options. That is something he can actually help with.
He sounds disappointed, but he is looking for a way forward.
A thoughtful change may help more than another exhausting practice session.
The post-match review has produced an actionable note for once.
The wings are fine. Perhaps the plan needs a different shape.
Check the available tools before blaming the operator. Sensible revision.
A bird can have more than one answer to trouble.
He is thinking about what to change. Hopefully he gives the birds some credit too.
I wonder which part of the battle made the missing option clear.

contexts.subject: Beck recommends moves matching the Pokemon's type for added power.

Route14_Text_BeckPostBattle.text: Try teaching POKéMON a move that's\nthe same type as it.\pThat apparently boosts the power\nof the move.$

replies.text: A move that feels at home gets a little extra bite. Useful.
Type affinity can improve a move's power. An important factor in selecting attacks.
Work with the partner's strengths. Good starting point.
That is a clear bit of advice to take from the battle.
It helps to know which tools a partner already handles especially well.
Sometimes the natural choice has a measurable advantage behind its elegance.
A small reward for doing what comes naturally.
Compatibility affects output. Always worth checking before optimizing the rest.
Some actions sit more comfortably in a creature's bones.
A useful rule, and simple enough to remember under pressure.
I wonder who first explained that trick to him.

contexts.subject: Marlon says he only wants to raise bird Pokemon.

Route14_Text_MarlonPostBattle.text: Bird POKéMON are my one true love.\nI don't want to raise anything else.$

replies.text: He found his people. His people happen to have feathers.
A narrow focus can produce deep knowledge of a particular group.
His choice. Best learn their weaknesses as well as the things he loves.
It is nice to hear someone so certain about what makes them happy.
A team you enjoy caring for is a good reason to keep learning.
An exclusive devotion, declared with absolutely no room for a non-winged understudy.
The world has many creatures. He knows which ones call him outside.
Specialization has benefits. A contingency plan still belongs in the kit.
Some people look up and find their whole answer there.
There is a difference between chasing a trend and knowing your own taste.
I wonder which bird made him decide this was his kind of team.

contexts.subject: Donald names Articuno, Zapdos, and Moltres as the three winged mirages.

Route14_Text_DonaldPostBattle.text: Well, the winged mirages are the\nlegendary bird POKéMON.\pThere are three of them: ARTICUNO,\nZAPDOS, and MOLTRES.$

replies.text: Three legendary birds. The sky has a very impressive guest list.
He can name the three legendary birds, though that does not establish their whereabouts.
Names are a start. Legends still deserve a careful approach.
The names make them feel a little more real than a vague story.
Interesting tale. We can keep listening without running after every rumor.
The winged mirages have acquired names, which only sharpens the mystery.
Three names that sound like weather people learned to whisper about.
Three distinct legendary birds! I would love to compare reliable observations.
Ice, lightning, flame. The sky keeps a varied household.
That is a much better explanation than just saying winged mirages.
I wonder how far those stories have traveled from their first witnesses.

contexts.subject: Benny says winning and losing are insignificant beneath the huge sky.

Route14_Text_BennyPostBattle.text: Winning, losing… It's insignificant\nunder this huge sky.$

replies.text: The sky has declined to keep score. Honestly, very considerate of it.
A wider frame can make a single result feel less consequential.
Fair enough. Still thank the team for the work.
Looking up can make a bad moment feel less crowded.
A little perspective after a hard match is no bad thing.
An immense celestial backdrop has been summoned for the post-match commentary.
The sky remains entirely unimpressed by both our records. Comforting.
Scale does change how a problem feels. Does not change the need to patch up afterward.
Above us, something vast is getting on with the afternoon.
A graceful thought, provided he remembers other people cared about the battle.
I wonder whether he felt that way before losing too.

contexts.subject: Lukas impatiently asks why we are still talking to him.

Route14_Text_LukasPostBattle.text: What, what, what?\nWhat do you want still?$

replies.text: He has enough whats for three conversations and wants none of them.
The repeated question suggests irritation rather than a request for detail.
Nothing else we need here. We can move on.
I do not think another answer would make this less awkward.
Best leave him a little room to cool down.
His vocabulary has narrowed while his volume remains ambitious.
A conversation stumbling over the same stone three times. We can leave.
Repeated warning signal. No extra troubleshooting needed.
The air around him has become rather prickly.
He is not in a listening mood. We do not need to stay.
He seems more upset that we remained than curious about what we want.

contexts.subject: Isaac complains that raising Pokemon is a drag.

Route14_Text_IsaacPostBattle.text: Raising POKéMON is a drag, man.$

replies.text: The Pokemon may also have notes about their working conditions.
Enjoying battle does not necessarily mean enjoying the sustained care training requires.
They depend on him. Boredom is no excuse to neglect them.
I hope he finds something about them that makes the effort feel worthwhile.
Caring for a team takes work. They still need him to show up.
He enjoys the premise and objects to the responsibilities in the fine print.
Living creatures are inconveniently unable to become hobbies only when we feel like it.
Ongoing maintenance is part of ownership. He cannot skip the whole section.
A companion is still there when the novelty goes quiet.
That is a rough thing to say while the team is standing nearby.
I wonder what made him want Pokemon before the daily work set in.

contexts.subject: Gerald praises our strong Pokemon and declares might makes right.

Route14_Text_GeraldPostBattle.text: It's cool you made your POKéMON so\nstrong.\pMight is right!\nAnd you know it!$

replies.text: Strong Pokemon, yes. A complete philosophy of justice, probably no.
Strength establishes capability. It does not establish whether a choice is justified.
Power tells you what you can do. Still have to choose well.
I am glad he respects the team. The rest makes me uneasy.
Being strong gives you more ways to help, too.
A compliment has wandered into a rather alarming political doctrine.
The biggest creature in a room does not automatically have the best idea.
Force solves some problems and creates plenty. It is not a universal tool.
A heavy hand can still point the wrong way.
He can admire the team without making every argument a contest of muscle.
I wonder how that rule sounds to him when someone stronger disagrees.

contexts.subject: Malik threatens that he could beat us in a personal fight.

Route14_Text_MalikPostBattle.text: You know who'd win, you and me\none-on-one!$

replies.text: He has proposed changing the entire sport until the result suits him. We can decline.
That threat is unrelated to the Pokemon battle and does not warrant engagement.
Stay close. We are leaving him right here.
That stopped sounding like a game. I would rather go.
No reason to let his embarrassment become somebody else's injury.
The defeated competitor has requested a new contest with markedly worse manners.
His pride would like to borrow our bruises. It can remain disappointed.
Unacceptable rule change. Best end the interaction.
Some people try to make their hurt into someone else's. Keep walking.
Losing did not grant him permission to threaten us.
He seems much more interested in recovering his pride than having a conversation.

contexts.subject: Kiri worries that the double-battle loss was her fault.

Route14_Text_KiriPostBattle.text: KIRI: Did we lose because of me?$

replies.text: Two people shared that battle. One person does not have to carry all the sad bits.
A team result has several causes. Assigning all responsibility to herself is premature.
She tried. That matters more than finding someone to blame.
I know how quickly a loss can start sounding like proof against yourself.
She needs a kind word before she needs a detailed battle review.
A shared defeat need not end with one partner appointed its sole author.
The mind can make a single loss unreasonably personal. I know the trick.
One result is not enough to isolate a cause. Especially with two trainers involved.
Two shadows crossed the field. One need not hold all the darkness afterward.
She is looking for blame when her partner might simply want another try together.
I hope she looks at Jan before deciding what Jan thinks.

contexts.subject: Jan comforts Kiri and proposes trying harder together next time.

Route14_Text_JanPostBattle.text: JAN: KIRI, don't cry!\nWe'll just try harder next time.$

replies.text: She kept the important part of the team standing: the part between them.
Reassuring a partner preserves the cooperation they will need for improvement.
Good response. Nobody learns much while being blamed for everything.
She noticed Kiri needed her more than the result needed explaining.
A next time together is a good thing to offer someone who feels awful.
The match ended badly; the partnership received a rather better ending.
A loss can leave room for an unexpectedly good friend to speak.
Team morale repaired before the next round of practice. Excellent priorities.
She is keeping a small light on for the next attempt.
A generous response, with no audience needed to make it count.
That tells us more about their partnership than the battle did.

contexts.subject: Raul recommends collecting and selling things found on Cycling Road.

Route17_Text_RaulPostBattle.text: You can find good stuff lying\naround on CYCLING ROAD.\pThere's good money in picking them\nup and selling them.$

replies.text: Roadside treasure hunting. Mind the part where a bicycle tries to become the treasure.
Recovering discarded useful items can be worthwhile if the road remains safe.
Watch the traffic before watching the ground.
It must take a patient eye to notice things while everyone else rushes past.
Useful finds are nice. Stepping into a rider's path would spoil the profit.
Cycling Road supports an unexpected salvage economy.
A living made from what hurried people fail to notice.
Recover, inspect, reuse. Sensible, provided the item is not someone's missing possession.
The road sheds little things as people travel through it.
A sharp eye can find value. It should also recognize something recently lost.
I wonder what the strangest useful thing he has found here was.

contexts.subject: Isaiah threatens to belly-bump us away after losing.

replies.text: An unusual threat. Still a threat, even with that much wobble in the wording.
Physical intimidation is not an appropriate extension of a lost battle.
No. Keep your hands and everything else to yourself.
That is enough of this conversation for me.
He can be disappointed without trying to knock people over.
An undignified tactic has been announced with considerable confidence.
I prefer my personal space without an incoming stomach.
Collision testing is neither requested nor necessary. Let's move on.
His pride seems to be looking for somewhere to land. We can step away.
He has confused taking up space with being entitled to ours.
That sounds like an excellent reason to give him a wide berth.

contexts.subject: Virgil enthusiastically describes racing downhill.

replies.text: Downhill does half the pedaling and all the tempting. Keep a hand on the brakes.
Gravity supplies acceleration; steering and braking remain the rider's responsibilities.
Enjoy the slope. Leave yourself enough room to stop.
He sounds happiest when he is moving. I understand the appeal.
A breeze after a hard climb must feel earned.
A whole hill conspires to make his favorite pastime more dramatic.
The road lends you speed and expects you to return it carefully.
Free acceleration! With a very important braking system attached.
For a moment, the hill does the work and the wind takes the credit.
There is a particular joy in a road that finally tilts your way.
I wonder whether he has a favorite stretch of the descent.

contexts.subject: Billy asks whether we are looking for adventure.

replies.text: Adventure keeps finding us before we finish looking for a bench.
That depends on what sort of adventure he has in mind. Details matter.
Depends. A good road is enough without someone manufacturing trouble.
I like a little uncertainty, when there is still time to get home safely.
An interesting route and decent company already count for quite a lot.
A broad invitation from a man beside a very long slope. Clarification advised.
Adventure is a lovely word until it starts explaining the bruises.
Possibly! I would like to see the plan before committing the equipment.
Sometimes the next bend offers enough strangeness for one afternoon.
He has the opening line. I am waiting for the actual proposal.
I wonder what he considers an adventure on a road he knows so well.

contexts.subject: Nikolas says he caught Voltorb in the abandoned Power Plant.

Route17_Text_NikolasPostBattle.text: I got my VOLTORB at the abandoned\nPOWER PLANT.$

replies.text: An abandoned Power Plant still had somebody at work. Round somebody.
An old electrical facility is a plausible habitat for Voltorb.
Useful lead. Abandoned does not mean safe to wander through.
That must have been an unsettling place to hear something moving.
I hope he was careful around whatever equipment remained inside.
The building retired from one purpose and acquired a rather lively tenant.
A little life in a place people left behind. With a dangerous temper, perhaps.
An electrical Pokemon in a Power Plant! The old equipment may still matter to it.
Some buildings keep a pulse after their workers leave.
A memorable place to meet a partner. Also a place to watch your step.
I wonder what first gave away that the round thing was a Pokemon.

contexts.subject: Zeek wonders whether some Pokemon need elemental stones to evolve.

Route17_Text_ZeekPostBattle.text: Maybe some POKéMON need element\nSTONES to evolve.$

replies.text: Some Pokemon apparently want a very specific rock before making a big decision.
Evolutionary triggers vary. Stones are relevant to some species, not a universal solution.
Check the species before buying a pocket full of expensive rocks.
It is worth asking before assuming every partner changes the same way.
A little research can save a lot of confused waiting.
The next stage of life may have a mineral requirement. Biology remains delightfully inconvenient.
A stone can look very ordinary until it belongs beside the right creature.
An external trigger! The compatibility details would be worth checking.
Some futures open only when the right small thing is brought near.
A useful possibility to investigate before deciding a Pokemon has stopped progressing.
I wonder which partner made him start considering stones.

contexts.subject: Jamal jokes that the battle must have made him lose weight.

Route17_Text_JamalPostBattle.text: I'm sure I lost weight there!$

replies.text: An intense battle can feel like a whole afternoon of exercise in one minute.
A change in effort or sweating is not a reliable measure of lasting weight change.
He worked hard. A rest matters more than guessing at the scale.
He sounds exhausted enough that a quiet moment would help.
Catch your breath first. The battle does not need a second scorecard.
The match has received an unexpected review from the fitness department.
An afternoon can leave you feeling lighter without the numbers agreeing.
One dramatic trial is a poor measurement. Hydration would be more immediately useful.
He seems to have left a considerable amount of energy on the field.
He could simply be pleased he put in the effort.
I wonder whether that was his plan for the afternoon or just his consolation.

contexts.subject: Corey urges us to be ready to fight for our beliefs.

Route17_Text_CoreyPostBattle.text: Be ready to fight for your beliefs!$

replies.text: I believe in choosing the right fight. That one saves a lot of running.
Conviction deserves examination as well as commitment. Certainty alone is not evidence.
Stand by what matters. Think before swinging at everything else.
Holding your ground can matter. So can listening long enough to understand someone.
There are ways to show you mean something without getting everybody hurt.
A stirring declaration, though I would like to inspect the beliefs before endorsing the battle.
A belief should survive a question before it demands a fight.
Worth checking whether the plan serves the principle or just the adrenaline.
Roots hold firm without striking at every passing foot.
A strong conviction looks better with a little judgment attached.
I wonder which belief he had in mind when he said that.

contexts.subject: Jaxon warns that the slope makes steering difficult.

Route17_Text_JaxonPostBattle.text: The slope makes it hard to steer.$

replies.text: The hill has opinions about where the bicycle goes. Keep yours louder.
Downhill speed can make small steering errors much more consequential.
Slow down before the bend. Correcting late is how people get hurt.
I appreciate a warning from someone who has already tried the road.
Better to take the descent steadily than turn it into a very fast mistake.
Gravity has taken an interest in the handlebars. An unwelcome collaborator.
The road can carry you faster than your confidence deserves.
Steering gets harder at speed. Good reason to test the brakes before the slope.
A downward road asks for more attention than effort.
That is useful advice, especially from someone staying here to practice.
I wonder which bend catches visiting cyclists off guard most often.

contexts.subject: William decides he needs sleep after the battle.

Route17_Text_WilliamPostBattle.text: I need to catch a few z's!$

replies.text: He has identified a problem best solved horizontally.
Fatigue is a good reason to stop, particularly before further cycling.
Get somewhere safe before sleeping. Tired riding is a bad idea.
A quiet rest sounds like the kindest end to this afternoon.
Food and a proper place to lie down could improve things considerably.
The day's ambitions have been revised to a single, sensible objective.
A nap is a perfectly respectable answer to a long road.
Low battery detected. Best recharge before using the steering system.
The afternoon has finally become heavier than his eyelids.
Good that he can admit it. Looking energetic is a tiring obligation.
I wonder how far he still has to get home.

contexts.subject: Richard thanks us for the battle and feels ready to swim.

Route19_Text_RichardPostBattle.text: Thanks, kid!\nI'm ready for a swim.$

replies.text: Apparently we were the warm-up. My warm-ups usually involve less being attacked.
He seems to regard the battle as preparation for his swim.
He sounds ready. Still needs to pay attention to the sea.
It is nice to finish a battle with a simple thank-you.
A cheerful start to his swim. I hope he has enough energy left for the return.
A courteous opponent departs toward a rather larger pool of challenges.
He has managed to keep the day light. Good for him.
Warm-up complete. The actual swimming still deserves its own precautions.
He is carrying the good mood straight into the water.
A little gratitude makes the whole encounter feel better.
I wonder whether he comes here for a swim every day.

contexts.subject: Reece warns us that Tentacool stings are painful.

Route19_Text_ReecePostBattle.text: Watch out for TENTACOOL.\nThey sting so painfully.$

replies.text: Pretty floating things have filed a formal objection to being bumped into.
A useful warning. Tentacool should be given space rather than treated as harmless drift.
Watch the water. Give them room.
That sounds like knowledge he would rather not have learned personally.
A warning like that is worth passing on before somebody gets hurt.
The sea's delicate decorations apparently come equipped with an emphatic boundary.
Something translucent can still make its presence very clear.
Hazard identified. Better to steer clear than test the warning.
The gentlest-looking thing in the water may still insist on distance.
He offered that warning without making fun of anyone. Helpful.
I wonder how easy they are to spot when the water is choppy.

contexts.subject: Matthew boasts that he can outswim even marine Pokemon.

Route19_Text_MatthewPostBattle.text: I can beat even marine POKéMON\nat swimming.$

replies.text: That is a bold challenge to make while most of the competitors live here.
The claim depends considerably on which marine Pokemon and over what distance.
Confidence is fine. Save enough energy to get back.
He sounds proud. I hope he knows the water as well as he knows his own pace.
Winning a race matters less than having enough left for the shore.
A visiting mammal has challenged the entire resident swimming profession.
The sea has an extensive roster of possible rebuttals.
I would want species, distance, current, and a reliable stopwatch before accepting that.
The creatures that sleep here may have a few advantages.
A wonderfully confident statement with a lot of water around it.
I wonder whether a Pokemon has ever actually accepted his challenge.

contexts.subject: Douglas points out islands visible across the sea.

Route19_Text_DouglasPostBattle.text: I see a couple of islands over\nyonder!$

replies.text: Land on the horizon! Always nice when the sea includes a place to stop being sea.
Visible land gives us a useful reference point, though distance over water can deceive.
Good landmark. Do not assume it is as close as it looks.
A little shape in the distance can make all this water feel less endless.
Worth keeping in sight while we watch our strength and the return route.
The horizon has finally supplied something with edges.
Faraway land looks peaceful when you cannot yet hear it.
Useful navigation reference. We should still account for the current.
The water has left a few small places for feet.
I like how a distant island can redirect an entire conversation.
I wonder what he can make out from here that we cannot yet see.

contexts.subject: David guesses that fishing is how to find sea Pokemon.

Route19_Text_DavidPostBattle.text: I guess you have to fish for sea\nPOKéMON.$

replies.text: The sea is full of Pokemon and he is still negotiating introductions.
Fishing is one method, though his statement sounds more tentative than comprehensive.
A rod is worth trying. Watch what is around you, too.
It is all right to be figuring things out as you go.
A suitable rod and some patience would give him a way to start.
Surrounded by an ocean, he has reached a cautiously nautical conclusion.
Sometimes an enormous habitat still leaves you wondering where to begin.
A testable idea. Better than standing here and wondering indefinitely.
A line is one small question you can lower into a large mystery.
He sounds uncertain rather than boastful. I appreciate that.
I wonder whether he has tried fishing here yet or is planning his first attempt.

contexts.subject: Tony watches the sea to take his mind off something bad that happened.

Route19_Text_TonyPostBattle.text: I'm looking at the sea to forget\nthe bad thing that happened!$

replies.text: The sea can do the talking for a while. He does not owe us the story.
A change of focus may offer relief. We need not ask for details he did not offer.
Let him have the view. We can give him some space.
Sometimes it helps to look at something that keeps moving without asking you to.
A quiet place and a little time can be enough company for now.
He has chosen an audience that will not interrupt or demand an explanation.
An immense thing going on with its day can be oddly good company.
No problem to solve for him unless he asks. We can leave him his quiet.
The water can hold a gaze without asking what brought it there.
He told us the boundary of the story. We should respect it.
I hope the shoreline gives him the pause he came here looking for.

contexts.subject: Anya is tired of the long journey toward Seafoam and wants to return to Fuchsia.

Route19_Text_AnyaPostBattle.text: It's still a long way to go to\nSEAFOAM ISLANDS…\pI want to go back to FUCHSIA…$

replies.text: Turning back is also a destination. A much more familiar one.
Recognizing fatigue before reaching the limit is a useful judgment.
Then turn back while there is energy left. The islands can wait.
She sounds homesick for shore more than curious about the islands now.
There is nothing wrong with choosing a shorter day than you planned.
The expedition has discovered that its finest destination may be the starting point.
Wanting home is good information when there is a lot of water left.
Revise the route before the energy budget reaches zero. Sensible.
A familiar shore can call louder than an unknown island.
An ambitious plan can change once you find out how it actually feels.
I wonder whether she has someone heading back with her.

contexts.subject: Alice explains that swimming to Seafoam was her boyfriend's idea.

Route19_Text_AlicePostBattle.text: My boyfriend wanted to swim to\nSEAFOAM ISLANDS.$

replies.text: His idea, their very long swim. I hope they both agreed on the return journey.
A shared outing still needs both people's limits considered.
His plan does not get to overrule her need for a rest.
The way she says it makes me wonder whether she wanted this trip herself.
A trip together works better when both people can say they have had enough.
The author of this itinerary appears to have recruited a second set of tired arms.
A romantic proposal can become considerably less romantic several miles offshore.
Shared project, separate energy reserves. Someone should have checked both.
One person's faraway wish can become another person's long way home.
I would like to know whether he asked what she wanted to do.
I wonder how differently they imagined this swim when they were still on land.

contexts.subject: Axle reports leg cramps while struggling in the water.

Route19_Text_AxlePostBattle.text: M-my legs! They cramped up!\nGlub, glub…$

replies.text: That is not a joke-shaped problem. He needs something solid to hold onto.
Cramping in the water is urgent. Help him reach flotation or nearby shore safely.
Get him support. Keep his head above water.
He sounds frightened. We should take that seriously right now.
He needs help getting out of the water before anything else.
The bravado ends here. A struggling swimmer needs help, promptly.
The sea is no place to hide that you are in trouble.
That needs immediate support, not another battle or a clever reply.
Something that floats needs to reach him before the words run out.
He is struggling. Somebody needs to help him toward safety.
He is having trouble staying up. We cannot treat that like ordinary post-battle chatter.

contexts.subject: Connie imagines riding Lapras to stay dry while crossing the sea.

Route19_Text_ConniePostBattle.text: If I were to ride a POKéMON on\nthe sea, I'd like a LAPRAS.\pLAPRAS is so big, I bet it\nwould keep me dry on water.$

replies.text: A sea journey with a seat. She has identified the important luxury.
Lapras's size makes the idea plausible, though waves would still be a factor.
A steady ride sounds better than exhausting yourself out here.
I understand wanting to enjoy the water without being entirely inside it.
A comfortable crossing and a dry change of clothes would make a lovely day.
She envisions nautical travel with a rather excellent seating arrangement.
The sea is beautiful from a place where it cannot immediately fill your shoes.
Buoyancy, room for a passenger, fewer wet belongings. Strong requirements list.
A gentle back between you and all that restless water.
Practical comfort is an underrated part of a good adventure.
I wonder whether she has ever met a Lapras close enough to see its size.

contexts.subject: Lia asks about a younger brother and hopes we teach him useful things.

Route19_Text_LiaPostBattle.text: LIA: Do you have a younger\nbrother?\pI hope you're teaching him all\nsorts of things.$

replies.text: She takes the big-sister job seriously. It apparently comes with a lesson plan.
Older siblings can provide a very influential model, deliberately or otherwise.
Teaching matters. Listening to the younger one matters too.
She sounds proud of having someone to look out for.
Sharing what you know is a good way to make a journey less frightening for somebody new.
An elder sister recruits the wider world into her informal educational program.
Small people remember what the larger familiar people bother to show them.
Passing on useful skills saves someone else from repeating every mistake.
A path is easier when someone points out the loose stones first.
She wants him prepared, rather than merely impressed. That is kind.
I wonder which little lesson her brother still talks about most.

contexts.subject: Luc admires his big sister for being both strong and kind.

Route19_Text_LucPostBattle.text: LUC: My big sis is strong and nice.\nI think she's awesome!$

replies.text: Strong and nice. That is a very good pair of things to be famous for.
He admires her conduct as well as her ability. An encouraging distinction.
Sounds like she has earned that trust.
He says it with no hesitation. That is a lovely thing to hear.
A younger sibling feeling safe and proud beside you is quite an achievement.
A concise and entirely devoted review from the person closest to the subject.
A small admirer who has chosen good things to admire.
Strength plus kindness. Finally, a specification with both essential features.
He has found someone whose shadow feels like shelter.
He notices that she is kind. Children are very good at knowing when it matters.
I wonder whether she knows he talks about her that way.

contexts.subject: Roger realizes his exhausted birds cannot fly him back.

Route20_Text_RogerPostBattle.text: My birds are exhausted.\nThey can't FLY me back!$

replies.text: The return ticket needs a rest. A rather important detail when it has wings.
Transport depends on the birds' remaining stamina. Their fatigue changes his options.
Rest them. Do not force a tired bird to carry you.
He sounds stranded. I hope there is somewhere safe for them all to recover.
A sheltered rest and time for the team would be the sensible next step.
The homeward journey has discovered that its transport also participated in the battle.
A way home can become a creature that needs you to wait.
The transport system shares the team's energy budget. Important planning lesson.
The wings that brought him here have earned a quiet place to fold.
He should have kept the return trip in mind. Now the birds need care.
I wonder whether he has a safe place to stop while they recover.
